claim: RasGRPs are guanine nucleotide exchange factors that are specific for Ras or Rap.
source: RasGRPs are guanine nucleotide exchange factors that are specific for Ras or Rap, and are important regulators of cellular signaling.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a general characterization of RasGRPs.

claim: RasGRPs are important regulators of cellular signaling.
source: RasGRPs are guanine nucleotide exchange factors that are specific for Ras or Rap, and are important regulators of cellular signaling.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a general characterization of RasGRPs.

claim: Aberrant expression or mutation of RasGRPs results in disease.
source: Aberrant expression or mutation of RasGRPs results in disease.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: The charge of His 212 in RasGRP1 alters signaling activity.
source: An analysis of RasGRP1 SNP variants led to the conclusion that the charge of His 212 in RasGRP1 alters signaling activity and plasma membrane recruitment, indicating that His 212 is a pH sensor that alters the balance between the inactive and active forms of RasGRP1.
evidence: This conclusion is based on experimental data from SNP variant analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The charge of His 212 in RasGRP1 alters plasma membrane recruitment.
source: An analysis of RasGRP1 SNP variants led to the conclusion that the charge of His 212 in RasGRP1 alters signaling activity and plasma membrane recruitment, indicating that His 212 is a pH sensor that alters the balance between the inactive and active forms of RasGRP1.
evidence: This conclusion is based on experimental data from SNP variant analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: His 212 is a pH sensor that alters the balance between the inactive and active forms of RasGRP1.
source: An analysis of RasGRP1 SNP variants led to the conclusion that the charge of His 212 in RasGRP1 alters signaling activity and plasma membrane recruitment, indicating that His 212 is a pH sensor that alters the balance between the inactive and active forms of RasGRP1.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by experimental data on pH modulation and His 212 mutations.

claim: The transition from the autoinhibited to the active form of RasGRP1 involves the rearrangement of an inter-domain linker that displaces inhibitory inter-domain interactions.
source: The transition from the autoinhibited to the active form of RasGRP1 involves the rearrangement of an inter-domain linker that displaces inhibitory inter-domain interactions.
evidence: This is based on structural comparisons between autoinhibited RasGRP1 and active RasGRP4:H-Ras and RasGRP2:Rap1b complexes.

claim: His 212 is located at the fulcrum of conformational changes between autoinhibited and active forms of RasGRP1.
source: His 212 is located at the fulcrum of these conformational changes, and structural features in its vicinity are consistent with its function as a pH-dependent switch.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis comparing autoinhibited and active forms.

claim: Structural features in the vicinity of His 212 are consistent with its function as a pH-dependent switch.
source: His 212 is located at the fulcrum of these conformational changes, and structural features in its vicinity are consistent with its function as a pH-dependent switch.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis and computational pKa predictions.

claim: Ras family of small G-proteins are molecular switches that transmit signals when bound to GTP.
source: The Ras family of small G-proteins, including Ras and Rap, are molecular switches that transmit signals when bound to GTP (Rojas et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Rojas et al., 2012.

claim: Son of Sevenless is a GEF that activates Ras.
source: Ras-family members are activated by specific guanine-nucleotide exchange factors (that we term GEFs for simplicity here), such as Son of Sevenless, that activates Ras (Boriack-Sjodin et al., 1998), and Epac1 and Epac2, that activate Rap (Rehmann et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Boriack-Sjodin et al., 1998.

claim: Epac1 and Epac2 activate Rap.
source: Ras-family members are activated by specific guanine-nucleotide exchange factors (that we term GEFs for simplicity here), such as Son of Sevenless, that activates Ras (Boriack-Sjodin et al., 1998), and Epac1 and Epac2, that activate Rap (Rehmann et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Rehmann et al., 2006.

claim: GEFs activate Ras-family members by triggering the release of GDP and its replacement by GTP.
source: GEFs activate Ras-family members by triggering the release of GDP and its replacement by GTP (Wittinghofer and Vetter, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wittinghofer and Vetter, 2011.

claim: There are four RasGRP proteins in humans.
source: One family of these GEFs is comprised of the Ras guanine-nucleotide releasing proteins (RasGRPs) that can activate Ras or Rap, of which there are four in humans.
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction.

claim: RasGRP1 is most extensively studied in T lymphocytes.
source: RasGRP1 is most extensively studied in T lymphocytes (Dower et al., 2000; Priatel et al., 2002; Roose et al., 2005; Daley et al., 2013), RasGRP2 in neutrophils and platelets (Lozano et al., 2016; Stone, 2011), RasGRP3 in B lymphocytes (Teixeira et al., 2003), and RasGRP4 in mast cells (Yang et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: RasGRP2 is most extensively studied in neutrophils and platelets.
source: RasGRP1 is most extensively studied in T lymphocytes (Dower et al., 2000; Priatel et al., 2002; Roose et al., 2005; Daley et al., 2013), RasGRP2 in neutrophils and platelets (Lozano et al., 2016; Stone, 2011), RasGRP3 in B lymphocytes (Teixeira et al., 2003), and RasGRP4 in mast cells (Yang et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lozano et al., 2016 and Stone, 2011.

claim: RasGRP3 is most extensively studied in B lymphocytes.
source: RasGRP1 is most extensively studied in T lymphocytes (Dower et al., 2000; Priatel et al., 2002; Roose et al., 2005; Daley et al., 2013), RasGRP2 in neutrophils and platelets (Lozano et al., 2016; Stone, 2011), RasGRP3 in B lymphocytes (Teixeira et al., 2003), and RasGRP4 in mast cells (Yang et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Teixeira et al., 2003.

claim: RasGRP4 is most extensively studied in mast cells.
source: RasGRP1 is most extensively studied in T lymphocytes (Dower et al., 2000; Priatel et al., 2002; Roose et al., 2005; Daley et al., 2013), RasGRP2 in neutrophils and platelets (Lozano et al., 2016; Stone, 2011), RasGRP3 in B lymphocytes (Teixeira et al., 2003), and RasGRP4 in mast cells (Yang et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Yang et al., 2003.

claim: RasGRPs can be found in epithelial lineages.
source: However, RasGRPs can be found in other cell types as well, including epithelial lineages (Depeille et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Depeille et al., 2015.

claim: T cell receptor or B cell receptor stimulation leads to an increase of diacylglycerol at the membrane.
source: T cell receptor (TCR) or B cell receptor (BCR) stimulation leads to an increase of diacylglycerol at the membrane, protein kinase C (PKC) activation, and increases in intracellular calcium levels (Myers and Roose, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Myers and Roose, 2016.

claim: T cell receptor or B cell receptor stimulation leads to protein kinase C (PKC) activation.
source: T cell receptor (TCR) or B cell receptor (BCR) stimulation leads to an increase of diacylglycerol at the membrane, protein kinase C (PKC) activation, and increases in intracellular calcium levels (Myers and Roose, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Myers and Roose, 2016.

claim: T cell receptor or B cell receptor stimulation leads to increases in intracellular calcium levels.
source: T cell receptor (TCR) or B cell receptor (BCR) stimulation leads to an increase of diacylglycerol at the membrane, protein kinase C (PKC) activation, and increases in intracellular calcium levels (Myers and Roose, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Myers and Roose, 2016.

claim: RasGRP1 is recruited to the plasma membrane where it binds diacylglycerol to enable interaction with Ras.
source: RasGRP1 is recruited to the plasma membrane, where it binds diacylglycerol to enable interaction with Ras.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as part of the mechanism of RasGRP1 activation.

claim: Upon receptor stimulation, RasGRP1 is phosphorylated by PKC.
source: Upon receptor stimulation, RasGRP1 is phosphorylated by PKC (Zheng et al., 2005; Roose et al., 2007), which enhances RasGRP1's GEF activity through unknown mechanisms.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Zheng et al., 2005 and Roose et al., 2007.

claim: PKC phosphorylation of RasGRP1 enhances RasGRP1's GEF activity through unknown mechanisms.
source: Upon receptor stimulation, RasGRP1 is phosphorylated by PKC (Zheng et al., 2005; Roose et al., 2007), which enhances RasGRP1's GEF activity through unknown mechanisms.
evidence: This is stated directly in the text, acknowledging that the mechanism is not yet understood.

claim: RasGRP1 contains a calcium-binding EF hand domain.
source: RasGRP1 contains a calcium-binding EF hand domain and calcium binding to RasGRP1 induces allosteric changes that release autoinhibition (Iwig et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: Calcium binding to RasGRP1 induces allosteric changes that release autoinhibition.
source: RasGRP1 contains a calcium-binding EF hand domain and calcium binding to RasGRP1 induces allosteric changes that release autoinhibition (Iwig et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Iwig et al., 2013.

claim: Alterations in RasGRP1 expression contribute to skin carcinoma.
source: Alterations in RasGRP1 expression contribute to diseases such as skin carcinoma (Diez et al., 2009; Luke et al., 2007), colorectal cancer (Depeille et al., 2015), and leukemia (Ksionda et al., 2016; Hartzell et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Diez et al., 2009 and Luke et al., 2007.

claim: Alterations in RasGRP1 expression contribute to colorectal cancer.
source: Alterations in RasGRP1 expression contribute to diseases such as skin carcinoma (Diez et al., 2009; Luke et al., 2007), colorectal cancer (Depeille et al., 2015), and leukemia (Ksionda et al., 2016; Hartzell et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Depeille et al., 2015.

claim: Alterations in RasGRP1 expression contribute to leukemia.
source: Alterations in RasGRP1 expression contribute to diseases such as skin carcinoma (Diez et al., 2009; Luke et al., 2007), colorectal cancer (Depeille et al., 2015), and leukemia (Ksionda et al., 2016; Hartzell et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ksionda et al., 2016 and Hartzell et al., 2013.

claim: Elevated RasGRP3 expression has been reported in prostate cancer.
source: Elevated RasGRP3 expression has been reported in breast cancer (Nagy et al., 2014), prostate cancer (Yang et al., 2010), lymphoma (Teixeira et al., 2003), cutaneous melanoma (Yang et al., 2011), and uveal melanoma (Chen et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Yang et al., 2010.

claim: Elevated RasGRP3 expression has been reported in lymphoma.
source: Elevated RasGRP3 expression has been reported in breast cancer (Nagy et al., 2014), prostate cancer (Yang et al., 2010), lymphoma (Teixeira et al., 2003), cutaneous melanoma (Yang et al., 2011), and uveal melanoma (Chen et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Teixeira et al., 2003.

claim: Elevated RasGRP3 expression has been reported in cutaneous melanoma.
source: Elevated RasGRP3 expression has been reported in breast cancer (Nagy et al., 2014), prostate cancer (Yang et al., 2010), lymphoma (Teixeira et al., 2003), cutaneous melanoma (Yang et al., 2011), and uveal melanoma (Chen et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Yang et al., 2011.

claim: Elevated RasGRP3 expression has been reported in uveal melanoma.
source: Elevated RasGRP3 expression has been reported in breast cancer (Nagy et al., 2014), prostate cancer (Yang et al., 2010), lymphoma (Teixeira et al., 2003), cutaneous melanoma (Yang et al., 2011), and uveal melanoma (Chen et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Chen et al., 2017.

claim: A polymorphism (Arg 519 Gly) in Rasgrp1 in mice results in T cell abnormalities and autoimmunity.
source: A polymorphism (Arg 519 Gly) in Rasgrp1 in mice results in T cell abnormalities and autoimmunity (Daley et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Daley et al., 2013.

claim: Several genetics studies have linked single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in RasGRP1 to human autoimmune disease.
source: Furthermore, several genetics studies have linked single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in RasGRP1 to human autoimmune disease (Plagnol et al., 2011; Qu et al., 2009), and low RasGRP1 levels have been detected in T lymphocytes from patients with Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) (Yasuda et al., 2007), and rheumatoid arthritis (RA) (Golinski et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Plagnol et al., 2011 and Qu et al., 2009.

claim: Low RasGRP1 levels have been detected in T lymphocytes from patients with Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE).
source: Furthermore, several genetics studies have linked single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in RasGRP1 to human autoimmune disease (Plagnol et al., 2011; Qu et al., 2009), and low RasGRP1 levels have been detected in T lymphocytes from patients with Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) (Yasuda et al., 2007), and rheumatoid arthritis (RA) (Golinski et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Yasuda et al., 2007.

claim: Low RasGRP1 levels have been detected in T lymphocytes from patients with rheumatoid arthritis (RA).
source: Furthermore, several genetics studies have linked single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in RasGRP1 to human autoimmune disease (Plagnol et al., 2011; Qu et al., 2009), and low RasGRP1 levels have been detected in T lymphocytes from patients with Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) (Yasuda et al., 2007), and rheumatoid arthritis (RA) (Golinski et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Golinski et al., 2015.

claim: Complete RasGRP1 deficiency in a patient leads to a novel primary immunodeficiency.
source: Complete RasGRP1 deficiency in a patient leads to a novel primary immunodeficiency, with impaired activation and proliferation of the patient's T- and B- cells and defective killing by cytotoxic T cells and NK cells (Roose, 2016; Salzer et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Roose, 2016 and Salzer et al., 2016.

claim: Complete RasGRP1 deficiency results in impaired activation and proliferation of T- and B- cells.
source: Complete RasGRP1 deficiency in a patient leads to a novel primary immunodeficiency, with impaired activation and proliferation of the patient's T- and B- cells and defective killing by cytotoxic T cells and NK cells (Roose, 2016; Salzer et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Roose, 2016 and Salzer et al., 2016.

claim: Complete RasGRP1 deficiency results in defective killing by cytotoxic T cells and NK cells.
source: Complete RasGRP1 deficiency in a patient leads to a novel primary immunodeficiency, with impaired activation and proliferation of the patient's T- and B- cells and defective killing by cytotoxic T cells and NK cells (Roose, 2016; Salzer et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Roose, 2016 and Salzer et al., 2016.

claim: Rasgrp2 deficiency in mice results in excessive bleeding.
source: Rasgrp2 deficiency in mice results in excessive bleeding, caused by defective platelets aggregation and degranulation (Crittenden et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Crittenden et al., 2004.

claim: Rasgrp2 deficiency in mice causes defective platelet aggregation and degranulation.
source: Rasgrp2 deficiency in mice results in excessive bleeding, caused by defective platelets aggregation and degranulation (Crittenden et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Crittenden et al., 2004.

claim: Polymorphisms in RasGRP2 cause a platelet disorder in patients.
source: Moreover, polymorphisms in RasGRP2, either converting Arg 113 into a stop codon, or missense mutations (Gly 248 Trp or Ser 381 Phe), cause a platelet disorder in patients (Lozano et al., 2016;Canault et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lozano et al., 2016 and Canault et al., 2014.

claim: The N-terminal portion of the RasGRPs contains the catalytic module that is common to other GEFs that operate on Ras-family members.
source: The N-terminal portion of the RasGRPs contains the catalytic module that is common to other GEFs that operate on Ras-family members (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The catalytic module of RasGRPs consists of a Ras-exchanger motif (REM) domain followed by a Cdc25 domain.
source: This module consists of a Ras-exchanger motif (REM) domain followed by a Cdc25 domain (Boguski and McCormick, 1993;Fam et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Boguski and McCormick, 1993 and Fam et al., 1997.

claim: The Cdc25 domain interacts with Ras and is responsible for nucleotide release.
source: As first revealed by structural analysis of the Ras-specific GEF Son-of-Sevenless (SOS), the Cdc25 domain interacts with Ras and is responsible for nucleotide release, and the REM domain provides structural support for the Cdc25 domain (Boriack-Sjodin et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Boriack-Sjodin et al., 1998.

claim: The REM domain provides structural support for the Cdc25 domain.
source: As first revealed by structural analysis of the Ras-specific GEF Son-of-Sevenless (SOS), the Cdc25 domain interacts with Ras and is responsible for nucleotide release, and the REM domain provides structural support for the Cdc25 domain (Boriack-Sjodin et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Boriack-Sjodin et al., 1998.

claim: RasGRP proteins contain a Ca2+-binding EF domain.
source: The remaining portion of the RasGRP proteins consists of a Ca2+-binding EF domain and a C1 domain that binds diacylglycerol for membrane localization (Beaulieu et al., 2007; Ebinu et al., 1998; Zahedi et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Beaulieu et al., 2007, Ebinu et al., 1998, and Zahedi et al., 2011.

claim: RasGRP proteins contain a C1 domain that binds diacylglycerol for membrane localization.
source: The remaining portion of the RasGRP proteins consists of a Ca2+-binding EF domain and a C1 domain that binds diacylglycerol for membrane localization (Beaulieu et al., 2007; Ebinu et al., 1998; Zahedi et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Beaulieu et al., 2007, Ebinu et al., 1998, and Zahedi et al., 2011.

claim: RasGRP1 has a C-terminal coiled-coil domain that is missing in the other family members.
source: RasGRP1 has a C-terminal coiled-coil domain that is missing in the other family members.
evidence: This is stated directly in the text.

claim: The common set of domains in RasGRP-1, -2, -3, and -4 show a high degree of sequence conservation.
source: The common set of domains in RasGRP-1, -2, -3, and -4 show a high degree of sequence conservation (Ksionda et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ksionda et al., 2013.

claim: In autoinhibited RasGRP1, the Cdc25-EF linker prevents Ras binding to the active site.
source: In unstimulated cells, RasGRP1 is in an inactive conformation, in which the Cdc25-EF linker prevents Ras binding to the active site (Iwig et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Iwig et al., 2013.

claim: In dimeric and autoinhibited RasGRP1, the EF domains from each molecule in a RasGRP1 dimer block the DAG-binding sites on the C1 domains of the dimer partner.
source: In dimeric and autoinhibited RasGRP1, the EF domains from each molecule in a RasGRP1 dimer block the DAG-binding sites on the C1 domains of the dimer partner (Figure 8).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 8.

claim: His 212 Tyr SNV signaled more strongly to ERK than WT RasGRP1.
source: However, the His 212 Tyr SNV signaled more strongly to ERK than WT, indicating altered regulation of RasGRP1.
evidence: This is based on experimental data from flow cytometry assays.

claim: His 212 Tyr resulted in increased basal signals to P-ERK and P-S6 in unstimulated cells as compared to WT RasGRP1.
source: More detailed analysis of the cellular biochemical traits of the SNVs in the His 212 region demonstrated that His 212 Tyr, but not Ser 220 Leu, Phe 221 Cys, and Phe 226 Leu, resulted in increased basal signals to P-ERK and P-S6 in unstimulated cells as compared to WT RasGRP1 (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: His 212 in RasGRP1 is conserved among all vertebrate RasGRPs.
source: His 212 in RasGRP1 is conserved among all vertebrate RasGRPs, and is present in most RasGRP proteins from lower organisms (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment shown in Figure 2A.

claim: His 212 is located in the first helix of the Cdc25 domain.
source: This residue is located in the first helix of the Cdc25 domain, and is far from the Ras-binding site.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis.

claim: His 212 is far from the Ras-binding site.
source: This residue is located in the first helix of the Cdc25 domain, and is far from the Ras-binding site.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis.

claim: His 212 Tyr and His 212 Ala showed increased basal signals to P-ERK in RasGRP1−/−RasGRP3−/− DT40 cells.
source: Analysis of the human SNV variant His 212 Tyr and His 212 Ala, both alterations to neutral residues, showed increased basal signals to P-ERK in RasGRP1−/−RasGRP3−/− DT40 cells (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) as well as in JPRM441 (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), a RasGRP1-deficient Jurkat T cell leukemia line that we previously exploited to asses RasGRP1 function (Roose et al., 2005; Iwig et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figures 2B and 2C.

claim: His 212 Tyr and His 212 Ala showed increased basal signals to P-ERK in JPRM441 cells.
source: Analysis of the human SNV variant His 212 Tyr and His 212 Ala, both alterations to neutral residues, showed increased basal signals to P-ERK in RasGRP1−/−RasGRP3−/− DT40 cells (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) as well as in JPRM441 (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), a RasGRP1-deficient Jurkat T cell leukemia line that we previously exploited to asses RasGRP1 function (Roose et al., 2005; Iwig et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figures 2B and 2C.

claim: His 212 Tyr and His 212 Ala variants signaled stronger to P-S6 in the DT40 cell system.
source: Similarly, the His 212 Tyr and His 212 Ala variants of RasGRP1 signaled stronger to P-S6 in the DT40 cell system (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C); PTEN- and SHIP1-deficiency in Jurkat results in hyperactive PI3kinase signals (Abraham and Weiss, 2004), making analysis of PI3K-dependent signals, such as those to S6, difficult in Jurkat.
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The His 212 Tyr and His 212 Ala variants are less autoinhibited.
source: Thus, the His 212 Tyr and His 212 Ala variants are less autoinhibited.
evidence: This is inferred from the increased basal signaling observed with these variants.

claim: Mutation of His 212 to positively charged residues (His 212 Arg and His 212 Lys) maintained autoinhibition of RasGRP1 activity in unstimulated cells with a similar efficiency as WT RasGRP1.
source: Mutation of His 212 to positively charged residues, i.e. His 212 Arg and His 212 Lys, maintained autoinhibition of RasGRP1 activity in unstimulated cells with a similar efficiency as WT RasGRP1 (Figures 2E,F and G, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D,E and F).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figures 2E, 2F, and 2G.

claim: Changing His 212 to neutral residues (His 212 Tyr or His 212 Ala) resulted in increased levels of BCR-induced phosphorylation of ERK and S6.
source: Changing His 212 to neutral residues, as in the human SNV His 212 Tyr or the designed His 212 Ala variant, resulted in increased levels of BCR-induced phosphorylation of ERK and S6 (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figures 3B and 3C.

claim: Altering His 212 to positively charged residues (His 212 Arg or His 212 Lys) impaired the BCR-induced ERK and S6 responses.
source: Conversely, altering His 212 to positively charged residues, either His 212 Arg or His 212 Lys, impaired the BCR-induced ERK and S6 responses (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figures 3D and 3E.

claim: Wildtype and His 212 Tyr versions of RasGRP1-EGFP revealed very similar efficiency of plasma membrane recruitment upon BCR-stimulation.
source: Wildtype and His 212 Tyr versions of RasGRP1-EGFP revealed very similar efficiency of plasma membrane recruitment upon BCR-stimulation (Figure 3F and G, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on microscopy data shown in Figures 3F and 3G.

claim: The His 212 Lys mutation resulted in complete lack of RasGRP1 plasma membrane recruitment.
source: Most striking was the complete lack of RasGRP1 plasma membrane recruitment for the positively charged mutant His 212 Lys (Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on microscopy data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The His 212 Lys mutation blocks the responsiveness of RasGRP1 to calcium and DAG cues.
source: Thus, the His 212 Lys mutation blocks the responsiveness of RasGRP1 to these calcium and DAG cues.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of membrane recruitment despite BCR stimulation.

claim: The positive charge of His 212 contributes to RasGRP1 autoinhibition in the basal state.
source: Together, these data suggest that the positive charge of His 212 contributes to RasGRP1 autoinhibition in the basal state (Figure 2), and that a neutral residue at position 212 is essential to allow for RasGRP1 plasma membrane recruitment and signal output to the ERK and S6 pathways (Figure 3).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data on His 212 mutations.

claim: A neutral residue at position 212 is essential to allow for RasGRP1 plasma membrane recruitment and signal output to the ERK and S6 pathways.
source: Together, these data suggest that the positive charge of His 212 contributes to RasGRP1 autoinhibition in the basal state (Figure 2), and that a neutral residue at position 212 is essential to allow for RasGRP1 plasma membrane recruitment and signal output to the ERK and S6 pathways (Figure 3).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data on His 212 mutations.

claim: Stimulation of DT40 cells by PMA and ionomycin resulted in a consistent increase of the intracellular pH.
source: Stimulation of DT40 cells by PMA (a diacylglycerol analogue) and ionomycin (calcium ionophore), mimicking lymphocyte receptor signaling events that connect to RasGRP1, resulted in a consistent increase of the intracellular pH (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Treating cells with 15 mM NH4Cl increased pHi.
source: In our transfected RasGRP1−/−RasGRP3−/− DT40 cells, treating with 15 mM NH4Cl increased pHi, whereas a NH4Cl pulse followed by EIPA treatment resulted in a trend towards decreased pHi (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: A NH4Cl pulse followed by EIPA treatment resulted in a trend towards decreased pHi.
source: In our transfected RasGRP1−/−RasGRP3−/− DT40 cells, treating with 15 mM NH4Cl increased pHi, whereas a NH4Cl pulse followed by EIPA treatment resulted in a trend towards decreased pHi (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: NH4Cl pretreatment resulted in augmentation of the BCR-induced ERK phosphorylation in RasGRP1−/−RasGRP3−/− DT40 cells that were transfected with WT RasGRP1.
source: NH4Cl pretreatment was compared to vehicle pretreatment, and resulted in augmentation of the BCR-induced ERK phosphorylation in RasGRP1−/−RasGRP3−/− DT40 cells that were transfected with WT RasGRP1 (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: NH4Cl + EIPA treatment did not increase BCR-induced ERK signaling, but resulted in a trend towards decreased ERK signals.
source: In contrast, NH4Cl + EIPA treatment did not increase BCR-induced ERK signaling, but resulted in a trend towards decreased ERK signals (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Increased pHi or decreased pHi only impacted the level of ERK signaling when His 212 in RasGRP1 was intact.
source: We found that increased pHi (Figure 4H) or decreased pHi (Figure 4I) only impacted the level of ERK signaling when His 212 in RasGRP1 was intact.
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figures 4H and 4I.

claim: His 212 Tyr and His 212 Lys lost the pHi-dependent regulation.
source: His 212 Tyr and His 212 Lys lost the pHi-dependent regulation.
evidence: This is based on experimental data comparing pH modulation effects on different His 212 variants.

claim: His 212 in RasGRP1 is a pH sensor.
source: These data indicate that His 212 in RasGRP1 is a pH sensor, and that increases in intracellular pH and His 212 deprotonation promote RasGRP1 activation.
evidence: This is the main conclusion based on pH modulation experiments.

claim: Increases in intracellular pH and His 212 deprotonation promote RasGRP1 activation.
source: These data indicate that His 212 in RasGRP1 is a pH sensor, and that increases in intracellular pH and His 212 deprotonation promote RasGRP1 activation.
evidence: This is the main conclusion based on pH modulation experiments.

claim: RasGRP1 and RasGRP4 are specific for Ras.
source: We found that RasGRP1 and RasGRP4 are specific for Ras, whereas RasGRP2 has a clear preference for Rap1B.
evidence: This is based on in vitro GEF assay data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: RasGRP2 has a clear preference for Rap1B.
source: We found that RasGRP1 and RasGRP4 are specific for Ras, whereas RasGRP2 has a clear preference for Rap1B.
evidence: This is based on in vitro GEF assay data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: RasGRP3 works equally efficiently as a GEF for Ras, Rap1B and Rap2A.
source: RasGRP3 works equally efficiently as a GEF for Ras, Rap1B and Rap2A (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is based on in vitro GEF assay data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The linker connecting the REM domain to the Cdc25 domain (REM-Cdc25 linker) is ordered in its entirety in the RasGRP2:Rap1B structure.
source: An intriguing aspect of the RasGRP2:Rap1B structure is that the linker connecting the REM domain to the Cdc25 domain (REM-Cdc25 linker) is ordered in its entirety (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: This is based on the crystal structure of RasGRP2:Rap1B.

claim: The REM-Cdc25 linker is disordered in the RasGRP4 structure.
source: By contrast, this linker is disordered in the RasGRP4 structure (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is based on the crystal structure of RasGRP4:HRas.

claim: The sequence of the REM-Cdc25 linker is conserved between RasGRP1 and RasGRP2.
source: The sequence of the linker is conserved between RasGRP1 and RasGRP2, but is drastically different in RasGRP4 (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The sequence of the REM-Cdc25 linker is drastically different in RasGRP4 compared to RasGRP1 and RasGRP2.
source: The sequence of the linker is conserved between RasGRP1 and RasGRP2, but is drastically different in RasGRP4 (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The structure of the REM-Cdc25 linker as visualized in the RasGRP2 structure is inconsistent with adoption of the autoinhibited structure of RasGRP1.
source: The structure of the linker as visualized in the RasGRP2 structure is of potential functional importance, because it is inconsistent with adoption of the autoinhibited structure of RasGRP1 that we have defined earlier (Iwig et al., 2013) (compare Figure 6A and B with Figure 6E).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison between active RasGRP2 and autoinhibited RasGRP1.

claim: In the structure of autoinhibited RasGRP1, the EF domain is docked on top of helix J of the Cdc25 domain.
source: In the structure of autoinhibited RasGRP1, the EF domain is docked on top of helix J of the Cdc25 domain (Figure 6E; the helices are labeled as defined for the Cdc25 domain of SOS [Boriack-Sjodin et al., 1998]).
evidence: This is based on the crystal structure of autoinhibited RasGRP1.

claim: In the structure of RasGRP2:Rap1B, the REM-Cdc25 linker runs along the surface of helix J, and wraps around it by forming an α helix.
source: In the structure of RasGRP2:Rap1B, the REM-Cdc25 linker runs along the surface of helix J, and wraps around it by forming an α helix (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is based on the crystal structure of RasGRP2:Rap1B.

claim: The high sequence conservation of the REM-Cdc25 linker between RasGRP1 and RasGRP2 suggests that the linker might adopt the same conformation in the active states of both molecules.
source: The high sequence conservation of the REM-Cdc25 linker between RasGRP1 and RasGRP2 suggests that the linker might adopt the same conformation in the active states of both molecules.
evidence: This is inferred from sequence conservation and structural data.

claim: Arg 181 mutation to alanine (Arg 181 Ala) resulted in somewhat lower levels of basal RasGRP1 signals to P-ERK.
source: Upon mutation of the ion-pairing residues, only Arg 181 mutation to alanine (Arg 181 Ala) resulted in somewhat lower levels of basal RasGRP1 signals to P-ERK (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Both Arg 181 Ala and Asp 228 Ala mutants revealed decreased induction of both P-ERK and P-S6 under BCR stimulatory conditions, in comparison to levels induced by wild type RasGRP1.
source: Both mutants (Arg 181 Ala and Asp 228 Ala) revealed decreased induction of both P-ERK and P-S6 under BCR stimulatory conditions, in comparison to levels induced by wild type RasGRP1 (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Formation of the ion pair between Arg 181 and Asp 228 is necessary for robust activation of RasGRP1.
source: Taken together, our results indicate that formation of the ion pair between Arg 181 and Asp 228 is necessary for robust activation of RasGRP1.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data on Arg 181 and Asp 228 mutations.

claim: PMA- or antigen receptor-induced phosphorylation of RasGRP1 at Thr 184 is correlated with increased RasGRP activity.
source: Another observation that points to the relevance of this linker conformation is that PMA- or antigen receptor-induced phosphorylation of RasGRP1 at Thr 184 in the REM-Cdc25 linker, or RasGRP3 at the corresponding residue (Thr 133), is correlated with increased RasGRP activity.
evidence: This is based on prior knowledge and observations.

claim: Mutation of Thr 184 to alanine results in reduced, but not eliminated, RasGEF activity.
source: Mutation of these threonine residues to alanine results in reduced, but not eliminated, RasGEF activity (Aiba et al., 2004), whereas introduction of a negative charge to mimic a phosphorylated threonine results in higher activity (Roose et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Aiba et al., 2004 and Roose et al., 2005.

claim: Introduction of a negative charge to mimic a phosphorylated threonine at position 184 results in higher RasGRP1 activity.
source: Mutation of these threonine residues to alanine results in reduced, but not eliminated, RasGEF activity (Aiba et al., 2004), whereas introduction of a negative charge to mimic a phosphorylated threonine results in higher activity (Roose et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Roose et al., 2005.

claim: Thr 134 in RasGRP2 is phosphorylated in lymphocytes.
source: The corresponding residue in RasGRP2 is Thr 134 (Figure 6D) and is phosphorylated in lymphocytes analyzed by total phospho-proteomics (Dr. Doreen Cantrell, set of 11 phospho-peptides from RasGRP2, personal communication).
evidence: This is based on personal communication with Dr. Doreen Cantrell.

claim: There are five negatively charged residues in the vicinity of His 212.
source: An unusual aspect of this histidine is that there are five negatively charged residues in its vicinity (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Four of the negatively charged residues near His 212 are provided by helix A (Glu 205, Glu 207, Glu 208 and Glu 211).
source: Four of these are provided by helix A (Glu 205, Glu 207, Glu 208 and Glu 211) and the fifth one (Glu 404) is provided by the loop leading into helix J, which packs against helix A (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Glu 404 is provided by the loop leading into helix J, which packs against helix A.
source: Four of these are provided by helix A (Glu 205, Glu 207, Glu 208 and Glu 211) and the fifth one (Glu 404) is provided by the loop leading into helix J, which packs against helix A (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 7E.

claim: The pKa value of His 212 is calculated to be 6.90.
source: Using the crystal structure of the cdc25 domain of RasGRP1 (Iwig et al., 2013), the pKa value of His 212 is calculated to be 6.90, that is, increased by almost 1 pH unit above the pKa value of an isolated histidine (6.0).
evidence: This is based on computational pKa prediction using continuum electrostatics.

claim: His 212 has the highest calculated pKa value among the nine histidines in the cdc25 domain.
source: His 212 has the highest calculated pKa value among the nine histidines in the cdc25, indicating that it is primed to convert from positive to neutral when the intracellular pH increases beyond a neutral value (Table 1).
evidence: This is based on computational pKa predictions shown in Table 1.

claim: The calculated pKa value of His 212 is reduced significantly when one or more of the four glutamate sidechains located nearby, in helix A, are substituted by alanine.
source: The calculated pKa value of this residue is reduced significantly when one or more of the four glutamate sidechains located nearby, in helix A, are substituted by alanine.
evidence: This is based on computational pKa predictions for mutants shown in Table 1.

claim: Mutation of Glu 404 resulted in altered RasGRP1 activity.
source: Consistent with this idea, we found that mutation of Glu 404 resulted in altered RasGRP1 activity, while mutation of Glu 208, located within helix A, had no effect.
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 7F and 7G.

claim: Mutation of Glu 208 had no effect on RasGRP1 activity.
source: Consistent with this idea, we found that mutation of Glu 404 resulted in altered RasGRP1 activity, while mutation of Glu 208, located within helix A, had no effect.
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 7F and 7G.

claim: Replacement of Glu 404 by either alanine or arginine both resulted in increased signals to S6 but not to the less basally active RasGRP1-ERK pathway.
source: Replacement of Glu 404 by either alanine or arginine both resulted in increased signals to S6 but not to the less basally active RasGRP1-ERK pathway (Figure 7F and G, and Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figures 7F and 7G.

claim: Lymphocyte receptor stimulation results in increased pHi, increased DAG levels, and increased intracellular calcium levels.
source: Lymphocyte receptor stimulation results in increased pHi, increased DAG levels, and increased intracelluar calcium levels, and we propose that these three signals coordinately induce a conformational change in RasGRP1.
evidence: This is based on prior knowledge and experimental observations in the manuscript.

claim: The three signals (increased pHi, increased DAG levels, and increased intracellular calcium levels) coordinately induce a conformational change in RasGRP1.
source: Lymphocyte receptor stimulation results in increased pHi, increased DAG levels, and increased intracelluar calcium levels, and we propose that these three signals coordinately induce a conformational change in RasGRP1.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental findings.

claim: The structure of the RasGRP2:Rap1B complex establishes an important role for the REM-Cdc25 linker in the transition to the active state.
source: The structure of the RasGRP2:Rap1B complex that we have now determined establishes an important role for the REM-Cdc25 linker in the transition to the active state.
evidence: This is based on the crystal structure of RasGRP2:Rap1B.

claim: A prominent feature in the active RasGRP2 structure is the formation of an ion-pair between Arg 131, in the REM-Cdc25 linker and Asp 177 in the Cdc25 domain.
source: A prominent feature in the active RasGRP2 structure is the formation of an ion-pair between Arg 131, in the REM-Cdc25 linker and Asp 177 in the Cdc25 domain (Arg 181 and Asp 228 in RasGRP1).
evidence: This is based on the crystal structure of RasGRP2:Rap1B.

claim: The salt bridge between Arg 131 and Asp 177 and the position of the REM-Cdc25 linker reinforces the active conformation of RasGRP and is incompatible with the autoinhibited conformation.
source: This salt bridge and the position of the REM-Cdc25 linker reinforces the active conformation of RasGRP and is incompatible with the autoinhibited conformation (Figure 7).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison between active and autoinhibited forms.

claim: The sequence of the REM-Cdc25 linker is conserved between RasGRP1, RasGRP2 and RasGRP3.
source: The sequence of the REM-Cdc25 linker is conserved between RasGRP1, RasGRP2 and RasGRP3 (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment shown in Figure 6D.

claim: RasGRP1, RasGRP2, and RasGRP3 share a common regulatory mechanism.
source: This suggests that these proteins share a common regulatory mechanism.
evidence: This is inferred from the sequence conservation of the REM-Cdc25 linker.

claim: The regulatory mechanism provides the first plausible structural explanation for how phosphorylation of Thr 184 in RasGRP1 results in a stable active conformation.
source: For RasGRP1, this mechanism provides the first plausible structural explanation for how phosphorylation of Thr 184 in RasGRP1 (Zheng et al., 2005; Roose et al., 2007) results in a stable active conformation (Figure 8).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis and prior knowledge of Thr 184 phosphorylation.

claim: The sequence of the REM-Cdc25 linker is divergent in RasGRP4.
source: The sequence of the REM-Cdc25 linker is divergent in RasGRP4, however, and the sequence of the EF domain indicates that RasGRP4 is unlikely to be regulated by calcium (Iwig et al., 2013; Reuther et al., 2002).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and citations.

claim: The sequence of the EF domain indicates that RasGRP4 is unlikely to be regulated by calcium.
source: The sequence of the REM-Cdc25 linker is divergent in RasGRP4, however, and the sequence of the EF domain indicates that RasGRP4 is unlikely to be regulated by calcium (Iwig et al., 2013; Reuther et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Iwig et al., 2013 and Reuther et al., 2002.

claim: The regulation of RasGRP4 is likely to be different from that of the other three members of the family.
source: Thus it appears that the regulation of RasGRP4 is likely to be different from that of the other three members of the family.
evidence: This is inferred from the divergent sequence of the REM-Cdc25 linker and EF domain in RasGRP4.

claim: Receptor signaling-induced increases in pHi is expected to convert His 212 to the deprotonated and neutral form.
source: Receptor signaling-induced increases in pHi is expected to convert His 212 to the deprotonated and neutral form, which destabilizes the autoinhibited conformation and potentiates the activation of RasGRP1 by calcium flux and DAG formation at the membrane (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental findings.

claim: Deprotonation of His 212 destabilizes the autoinhibited conformation and potentiates the activation of RasGRP1 by calcium flux and DAG formation at the membrane.
source: Receptor signaling-induced increases in pHi is expected to convert His 212 to the deprotonated and neutral form, which destabilizes the autoinhibited conformation and potentiates the activation of RasGRP1 by calcium flux and DAG formation at the membrane (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental findings.

claim: His 212 is predicted to have an increased pKa value, which is likely influenced by the adjacent cluster of glutamate residues.
source: His 212 is predicted to have an increased pKa value, which is likely influenced by the adjacent cluster of glutamate residues.
evidence: This is based on computational pKa predictions and structural analysis.

claim: Experimental work has shown that histidines with coordinating glutamate residues have upshifted pKa values when determined experimentally by NMR.
source: Supporting this idea, experimental work has shown that histidines with coordinating glutamate residues have upshifted pKa values when determined experimentally by NMR (Tishmack et al., 1997; Hiebler et al., 2017; Baran et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Tishmack et al., 1997, Hiebler et al., 2017, and Baran et al., 2008.

claim: Mutation of His 212 to non-titratable residues abrogates pH sensitive activation.
source: However, the fact that mutation of His 212 to non-titratable residues abrogates pH sensitive activation, strongly suggests that His 212 is essential for the pH-sensitive function of RasGRP.
evidence: This is based on experimental data on His 212 mutations.

claim: His 212 is essential for the pH-sensitive function of RasGRP.
source: However, the fact that mutation of His 212 to non-titratable residues abrogates pH sensitive activation, strongly suggests that His 212 is essential for the pH-sensitive function of RasGRP.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data on His 212 mutations.

claim: Increased pHi is a hallmark of cancer cells and promotes cancer progression.
source: More clear is the notion that increased pHi is a hallmark of cancer cells and promotes cancer progression (Webb et al., 2011; White et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Webb et al., 2011 and White et al., 2017.

claim: In drosophila models, increased pHi is sufficient to induce dysplasia, and it potentiates growth and invasion.
source: For example, in drosophila models, increased pHi is sufficient to induce dysplasia, and it potentiates growth and invasion (Grillo-Hill et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Grillo-Hill et al., 2015.

claim: RasGRP1 expression levels are increased in T cell leukemia (T-ALL) cells from patients.
source: In the light of cancer, it is of interest to note that RasGRP1 expression levels are increased in T cell leukemia (T-ALL) cells from patients (Hartzell et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hartzell et al., 2013.

claim: In T-ALL cell lines with increased RasGRP1 expression, RasGRP1 is constitutively recruited to the membrane where it constantly exchanges the nucleotide on Ras.
source: When we biochemically characterized these T-ALL cell lines with an increased level of RasGRP1 expression we noted that RasGRP1 is constitutively recruited to the membrane where it constantly exchanges the nucleotide on Ras (Ksionda et al., 2016; Hartzell et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ksionda et al., 2016 and Hartzell et al., 2013.

claim: RasGRP1 demonstrates constitutive phosphorylation on Thr 184 in T-ALL cells.
source: In agreement, RasGRP1 demonstrates constitutive phosphorylation on Thr 184 in these T-ALL cells (Ksionda et al., 2016) arguing that RasGRP1 spontaneously adopts an active conformation.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ksionda et al., 2016.

claim: An elevated pHi in cancerous T-ALL cells facilitates opening up of the overexpressed RasGRP1 leading to the constitutively high level exchange activity.
source: We speculate that an elevated pHi in these cancerous T-ALL cells facilitates opening up of the overexpressed RasGRP1 leading to the constitutively high level exchange activity that we observed (Ksionda et al., 2016; Hartzell et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the findings of the study.
